#597. The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

The way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A new study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.

Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.

The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.

"The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," said Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy shows up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.

"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction."

What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy

The researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.

To investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about important moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.

After writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.

The analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.

Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language

Participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.

Meanness, however, showed a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.

Boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.

These differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.

"What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane said. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.

"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life."

Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.

This variation is important because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.

"People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray said. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.

"Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships."

Like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.

This approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.

How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment

Recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.

"That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane said. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict important outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.

"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's important to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict."

Researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.

"If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she said. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions."

#594. A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics

A mysterious twist in the universe's oldest light could offer clues to physics that scientists have yet to discover. But before researchers can determine whether this subtle signal reveals something extraordinary about the cosmos, they must answer a crucial question: Is the effect actually coming from the universe, or could it be an illusion created by the telescopes observing it?

The mystery centers on the cosmic microwave background (CMB), a faint glow of radiation left over from approximately 380,000 years after the Big Bang. This ancient light provides a remarkable snapshot of the "baby universe" as it existed nearly 13.8 billion years ago, allowing scientists to investigate conditions from the earliest stages of cosmic history.

When the universe was about 380,000 years old, it had cooled enough to become transparent, allowing light to travel freely through space. As radiation scattered off free electrons during this transition, it acquired a small amount of linear polarization. Polarization describes the direction in which light's electric field oscillates, and a similar effect occurs when sunlight scatters through Earth's atmosphere.

Now, observations suggest that the polarization of this ancient radiation may have shifted slightly as the light traveled across the universe. This possible rotation, called cosmic birefringence, is especially intriguing because it could point to physical processes not explained by the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions. Confirming the effect might even provide new insights into dark matter and dark energy (see Sidebar).

A Mysterious Cosmic Signal or a Telescope Error?

There is a major obstacle to interpreting this potential discovery. An extremely small error in how a telescope's polarization detectors are aligned can produce a signal that looks almost identical to cosmic birefringence.

To help address this problem, physicists at the University of California San Diego developed a new technique for checking how accurately different groups of detectors measure polarization angles. They tested their approach using existing observations collected by the European Space Agency's Planck satellite, which mapped the universe's ancient radiation in extraordinary detail.

The research was led by Postdoctoral Fellow Anto I. Lonappan, Chancellor's Distinguished Professor of Physics Brian Keating, and Associate Professor of Physics Kam Arnold. Their findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Separating Real Cosmic Effects From Instrument Errors

Previous studies have suggested that the polarization of the CMB may have rotated by just a fraction of a degree over its nearly 14 billion years of travel. Although that sounds insignificant, such a tiny change could have enormous implications for fundamental physics.

Unfortunately, a telescope whose polarization detectors are misaligned by a similarly small angle could produce precisely the same apparent rotation. If every detector shares the same alignment error, the resulting measurements cannot distinguish that error from a genuine rotation of the cosmic signal.

The UC San Diego researchers found a way to investigate the problem from another angle. Rather than relying on a single combined measurement, they compared separate polarization maps generated by different groups of detectors.

If cosmic birefringence is real, its effect should appear consistently across all these maps. By comparing the maps with one another, the researchers can effectively eliminate any rotation shared by all of them. What remains reveals differences in the calibration of the individual detector groups, making it possible to identify inconsistencies that might otherwise complicate the search for new physics.

"The signal we are looking for is incredibly small, so we have to be certain that we are seeing the universe and not our instrument," said Lonappan. "Our method gives us a complementary way to check that distinction. Before interpreting a tiny rotation as new physics, we want to know that the calibration itself can be trusted."

Testing the Mystery With Planck Satellite Data

To evaluate their technique, the researchers analyzed eight polarization maps produced using Planck observations. They then compared their findings with results from an established approach called the Minami-Komatsu analysis, which is used to distinguish instrumental rotation from possible cosmic birefringence.

Although the two methods rely on different assumptions, they produced consistent results. This agreement provides an important independent check on how relative detector calibration errors are being assessed.

The new approach also has a deliberate limitation. Because it removes any rotation common to all the maps, it cannot independently measure the overall polarization angle or determine how much the universe itself may have rotated the light. Establishing that absolute rotation still requires an independent reference for calibrating the overall angle.

To demonstrate how their findings fit with existing measurements, the researchers combined their reconstruction of relative calibration differences with the common calibration value inferred from the established analysis. This produced an estimated cosmic birefringence angle of 0.37 ± 0.12 degrees, matching the Minami-Komatsu result.

Importantly, this agreement does not independently confirm that the ancient light has actually rotated. Instead, it shows that the new method can reproduce results from the existing framework while providing a separate way to examine potential calibration problems.

Searching for Gravitational Waves From the Early Universe

The technique could also play an important role in another major pursuit in cosmology: the search for gravitational waves generated during the universe's earliest moments.

To understand why, scientists distinguish between two patterns of polarization in the cosmic microwave background, known as E modes and B modes.

E modes were first detected in 2002. They arise from density variations in the early universe and form symmetric polarization patterns. B modes have a different appearance, featuring patterns that resemble curls or swirls.

One known source of B modes is gravitational lensing, which occurs when the gravity of matter between Earth and the early universe bends and distorts the path of ancient light. Scientists have already observed B modes created through this process.

However, researchers are also searching for a different kind of B mode that could have been produced by primordial gravitational waves. These ripples in spacetime may have originated during an extremely early period of rapid cosmic expansion, known as inflation. The distinctive B mode signal associated with those primordial gravitational waves has not yet been detected.

Finding it would provide powerful evidence about gravitational waves in the early universe and could offer strong support for particular models of cosmic inflation, potentially transforming scientists' understanding of how the universe began.

Why Extremely Precise Measurements Matter

The challenge is that even a slight error in a telescope's polarization calibration can cause some of the much stronger E-mode signal to appear incorrectly as B modes. This contamination could make an instrumental artifact look like an exciting cosmological discovery.

The UC San Diego method could help prevent such mistakes by identifying differences in polarization angle calibration among detector groups. That makes it a potentially valuable tool for future experiments searching for the extremely faint signatures of primordial gravitational waves.

This kind of independent verification will become increasingly important as observatories develop the ability to measure cosmic polarization with greater precision. One example is the Simons Observatory, where Keating serves as principal investigator.

As these instruments become more sensitive, researchers will need equally rigorous methods for confirming that the faint signals they detect are genuine features of the universe rather than imperfections in their equipment.

"The detection of primordial B modes would transform our understanding of the early universe, so the measurement must survive rigorous calibration checks," said Keating. "Anto has developed a useful new framework for testing relative polarization-angle calibration. This is ultimately about knowing when we can trust a measurement."

Beyond the Standard Model: Dark Matter and Dark Energy

The possibility of cosmic birefringence is particularly fascinating because it could reveal physics that lies beyond the Standard Model.

Although this framework has been remarkably successful at describing fundamental particles and their interactions, it cannot explain everything in the universe. Among its most important unanswered questions are the identity of dark matter and the origin and observed magnitude of dark energy. Together, these mysterious components account for approximately 95% of the universe's total energy density.

One possible explanation for cosmic birefringence involves a hypothetical field associated with particles resembling axions. Such a field could interact with light and gradually alter its polarization as it crosses the universe. However, these particles have not been confirmed to exist, and they would not necessarily be responsible for dark matter.

Other theoretical explanations connect the possible rotation to fields associated with dark energy, the mysterious phenomenon linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe.

If cosmic birefringence is eventually confirmed, it could provide an entirely new way to investigate these cosmic mysteries and reveal evidence of physical laws beyond those currently understood.

For now, the first challenge is ensuring that the subtle signal can be trusted. By giving researchers another way to identify potential measurement errors, the new technique strengthens the foundation for future discoveries that could reshape our picture of the universe.

#593. Fossil CEO says turnaround is ahead of plan as sales return to growth

Fossil Group posted quarterly results on Tuesday that could point to early signs of a turnaround for the legacy watchmaker.

The company, which has struggled to compete with new gadgets in the years since its sales and stock price peaked in the 2010s, has been quietly undertaking a comeback strategy under CEO Franco Fogliato. The company's fiscal third-quarter earnings indicate the strategy is beginning to bear fruit.

The company said Tuesday that it returned to profitability in the third quarter, posting operating income of $25.3 million, compared with an operating loss of $21.7 million last year. It also returned to sales growth, with net sales up 0.4% to $271.2 million. The company last reported a year-over-year sales increase in the first fiscal quarter of 2022.

"We're excited about improving dramatically the profitability of the company through a very strong and disciplined management of full-price sales as well as cost management," Fogliato told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

For the quarter ended Oct. 3, Fossil reported net income of $11.7 million, or 19 cents per share, compared with a net loss of $39.9 million, or 76 cents per share, the year prior. The company also said its operating expenses fell 11.1% to $137 million. The company last posted quarterly net income in the third fiscal quarter of 2022.

With the signs of growth, the retailer also raised its full-year outlook, guiding for full-year net sales of between $980 million and $990 million, which would mark a slight decline from just over $1 billion in net sales in the prior year. That compares with a previous expectation of net sales falling between 3% and 5%. Fossil also said it's expecting positive free cash flow by the end of the year.

Fogliato said Fossil had previously not expected sales growth for another year and a half.

The stronger quarter comes after the company saw slumping sales and financial losses over the past few years. It struggled with the rise of smartwatches, mounting debt and the decline in mall foot traffic.

Fossil stock has lost the vast majority of its value since the early-to-mid 2010s, and despite a recent surge, was trading under $8 a share on Tuesday.

To rightsize the business, Fogliato, who joined Fossil in 2024, said he focused on closing stores, moving away from promotions to full-price sales, improving marketing and broadening Fossil's product range. That meant shrinking the business to a sustainable baseline before trying to grow it.

The company saw a 5.9% decrease in direct-to-consumer sales for its third quarter, which Fogliato attributed to the company's "aggressive" downsizing.

"We simplified a lot of the business doing this," Fogliato said, adding that customers responded well when the company moved away from markdowns. "People tell me they are excited about what they are seeing in the marketplace now."

Fossil added that its key growth engine for the quarter was Asia, where net sales grew 15.1%. Fogliato said much of that growth was led by the India market.

At the same time, growing internationally is only part of the watchmaker's strategy as it tries to improve its performance in its home country.

"Priority number one is to grow our home market, and we're doing that," he said. "As retail is settling into a smaller, more profitable base, ready to grow again, we're entering 2027 with plenty of opportunities."

Fogliato said one key to growth was not trying to keep up with the smartwatch trend. While trying to make gains in the smartwatch space initially hampered Fossil's performance, it's now investing in analog watches again.

Smartwatch sales came in under $1 million for the quarter, but sales for traditional watches — which make up around 86% of Fossil's sales — grew 6.4%.

"Fossil is literally having a comeback, a strong comeback, a momentum, and we can see this," Fogliato said. "And it comes not only through the numbers — it comes with the excitement we see in the stores, and we think we're just at the beginning. We have so much work to do."

#592. The iPhone Duo Is Getting a Limited Version of Face ID

Apple's most expensive smartphone—the iPhone Duo—lacks one of the company's hallmark features: Face ID. The folding phone is already jam-packed with a hinge and multiple display layers, leaving no room for the TrueDepth sensor required for biometric face authentication. The Duo relies on Touch ID instead.

That's changing now in a software update. On Monday, Apple announced that it's bringing facial recognition to the iPhone Duo as part of the iOS 27.3 developer beta update. But since it can't rely on the tried-and-true Face ID system without those crucial components, it's borrowing the feature from the company's recently launched smart display, the HomeView.

The HomeView personalizes the display content for up to six people in a household, with its camera recognizing people who step in front of it. (It also uses voice data for recognition when someone asks Siri a command.) This “person recognition” technology is protected by the Secure Exclave—different from the Secure Enclave chip that houses Face ID data—a memory-protected space in Apple's A20 Pro processor. As WIRED's Lily Hay Newman writes, it's still not as comprehensive as Face ID, and could be more susceptible to attacks.

At launch, the iPhone Duo relied on Touch ID for biometric authentication.

Rumors abound that Apple is racing to add proper Face ID to the second-generation iPhone Duo. Still, tight development cycles might mean the feature may not arrive until the third generation in 2028. That also points to limitations in the Duo's new face recognition tech.

You cannot use it to authenticate payments or unlock sensitive content, like your banking app. You'll still need your thumbprint or passcode to approve Apple Wallet purchases. Instead, it's designed to unlock the foldable without tapping a finger on the Touch ID sensor. There is also a time-based limitation. For face recognition to work, it needs a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication within a 45-minute window. This capability is also restricted to the front screen and camera—it doesn't work if the iPhone Duo is unfolded. Also in iOS 27.3, Apple has a new toggle that lets you lock your iPhone Duo when you close it.

Google's newer Pixel folding phones are the only ones on the US market with secure facial authentication, though it's not as effective in the dark as Apple's Face ID. Samsung's facial biometrics on its Galaxy phones aren't strong enough to protect sensitive content and are largely used to unlock the device.

Apple’s willingness to roll out a watered-down version of Face ID is a rare compromise for the company—and shows just how much of a friction point Touch ID has become for Duo owners.

#590. NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos

"The first thing we said was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges."

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

When DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an important part of Hera's investigation.

ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify."

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit

Although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's new image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

The experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact

After a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

While DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

The findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

"Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!"

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

Materials provided by European Space Agency (ESA). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#588. Measles is surging in the U.S. — and outbreaks can cost millions

Measles outbreaks aren't just a public health threat. They can also be a financial burden on the U.S. — and the cost could only deepen as the once-eliminated disease spreads more widely.

The U.S. is expected to lose its official measles elimination status following a review by the Pan American Health Organization this week, after cases ratcheted to recent highs this year.

More than 5,100 measles cases have been reported nationwide in 2026 as of early November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. Eight deaths associated with the disease have been confirmed by states so far in 2026: six in Pennsylvania, one in New York and one in Wisconsin.

Based on this year's case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses.

The tool also estimates that 2025 measles outbreaks in the U.S. — which involved 2,289 confirmed cases nationwide – carried an economic cost of more than $37 million.

The costs extend beyond treating people who become sick, accounting for the resources health departments spend investigating and containing outbreaks, as well as wages lost when people have to miss work. The tool uses more recent, state-specific cost and financing data than an initial study by the researchers, which relied on historical outbreak costs.

The estimates from the tool are not a definitive accounting of what the outbreaks actually cost. But it illustrates the hefty bill tied to the spread of a disease that can be prevented through vaccination, and the potential economic consequences of falling childhood immunization rates. CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases.

"We're starting to see a whole bunch of people who decided not to get vaccinated as kids or have never gotten exposed to measles because they benefited from herd immunity, who now make it into adulthood and risk potentially getting quite seriously ill and requiring very significant medical expenses, or dying at the hospital," Bryan Patenaude, a health economist at the International Vaccine Access Center at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, who helped develop the tool, said in an interview.

Measles outbreaks can trigger a costly public health response, even when many people who are exposed never become sick.

When a case is identified, public health officials must investigate the infection, identify and notify people who may have been exposed, coordinate with hospitals and schools, and sometimes organize vaccination campaigns to prevent further spread. Those efforts can divert staff and resources from other public health priorities.

Costs could differ heavily depending on the state.

Johns Hopkins' data includes national averages alongside state-specific inputs, including inpatient hospital costs and wages from government data or trusted health policy sources. In New York, for example, the average inpatient hospital stay is roughly $4,200 a day, while the minimum wage is $16 per hour.

The tool estimates that the 48 cases reported by New York in 2025 carried an estimated $1.1 million in costs, including nearly $749,000 in public health responses, $333,000 in productivity losses and roughly $24,500 in direct medical expenses.

Meanwhile, the 803 cases in Texas, the epicenter of the largest U.S. measles outbreak in 2025, carried estimated costs of nearly $13 million, according to the tool. That includes $9 million in public health costs, $4 million in productivity losses and around $288,000 in direct medical expenses.

The tool builds on a study published by Patenaude and other researchers in August, which examined the costs of measles outbreaks in the U.S. The researchers reviewed published studies and government reports to compile historical estimates of medical expenses and public health response costs across 18 states.

The paper estimated that outbreaks carried a historical average cost of nearly $59,000 per case, just from the public health response. The researchers also estimated how costs scale with outbreak size, separating fixed up-front response expenses from the additional costs associated with each new case.

"A lot of this is incurred up front, and that's because of the human labor that's involved in contact tracing and all of the different actors that sort of need to be mobilized to deal with the fact that there's an outbreak," Patenaude told CNBC. "It's a largely labor-driven cost."

That model estimated roughly $298,000 in fixed costs and about $16,300 for each additional case. But it relied on historical data, including a particularly large 2019 outbreak in New York City, where contact-tracing labor costs were high. The researchers also excluded productivity losses from that model because most of the historical studies they reviewed did not consistently account for them.

The economic burden of measles extends beyond the costs of treating infected patients and organizing a public health response.

People who are exposed to measles may have to quarantine, even if they never develop symptoms. Parents can also be forced to miss work to care for sick or exposed children, while workers who contract the disease may lose wages during their recovery.

A 2025 study by Joey Mattingly, a pharmacist and health economist at the University of Utah, used published epidemiological and cost data to model the potential economic burden of a hypothetical 1,500-case outbreak. His analysis included direct medical expenses, public health spending and lost productivity, and examined how the estimates changed under different assumptions, including hospitalization rates.

The study estimated that the hypothetical outbreak could cost about $90 million, including roughly $26 million in productivity losses.

Those indirect costs can add up quickly because measles is highly contagious and a single infected person can expose dozens of others. Those contacts may need to quarantine or miss work while health officials determine whether they have been infected, creating costs even when they never develop the disease.

Mattingly estimated that each person who is quarantined could amount to roughly $300 in lost productivity alone.

If a single measles case exposes 40 to 50 people who then need to quarantine, that could translate into an estimated $12,000 to $15,000 in lost productivity, even if none of those contacts become sick.

That ripple effect is one reason Mattingly argues that the economic costs of outbreaks can quickly outweigh the investment required to vaccinate people against measles.

"Even if you don't get the infection, the contact costs you," he said. "And so it's just showing that there's this multiplication or exponential growth on the economic side that happens."

The financial burden can also fall unevenly across communities. While the costs of responding to an outbreak may be shared among local, state and federal agencies, Mattingly said the impact is often felt directly by local health departments.

"It's not like your health department is sitting around waiting for measles outbreaks," he said. "They're working, doing all these other things, and imagine having to just drop what you're doing because there's been a huge outbreak in the community."

Patenaude said the findings could help state and local health departments better anticipate the resources needed to contain outbreaks — particularly as measles cases continue to rise.

"It's not super expensive to treat and deal with a single case of measles compared to a single case of cancer," he said. "But if you have these outbreaks popping up and you're having to constantly divert resources that could be spent elsewhere by state and local health departments on measles, then you're going to wind up spending a lot of money very quickly."

#587. Microsoft outage cause revealed: It was a perfect storm of problems

You're probably aware that Microsoft 365, the popular suite of products that includes Outlook, suffered a massive global outage last week. In fact, it was the worst outage of the year, by a sizable margin. The problem took the computer giant roughly 24 hours, over the course of two business days, to get everything back up and running.

Aside from wondering when their email would be working again, the number one question on everyone's mind was what in the world happened to keep Microsoft 365 down for so long?

Now, we know. In a statement shared with customers and on X, Microsoft explained there were actually three causes, which created a perfect storm.

First, a bug caused servers to become unresponsive in specific conditions; second, an issue with Microsoft Teams increased server traffic and created those conditions; and third, many additional servers were already offline from an unrelated issue.

As Microsoft explained, on their own, neither issue would have caused such a large-scale problem. However, together, well, they kept one of the world's biggest tech companies scrambling for two days to fix their service.

In a social media post published on X, Microsoft's EVP of Copilot, Agents, and Platform Charles Lamanna explained the situation in detail.

According to Lamanna, a "latent defect" resulted in the company's servers becoming "overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions." The defect that caused the problem was introduced to Microsoft's systems during a July 2026 update as part of a fix for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers.

For months, as Lamanna described it, the issue went undetected, and it didn't cause any problems under normal load during Microsoft's testing process.

The second problem occurred when a surge in server load set off the defect. Lamanna says that Microsoft maintains two independent network gateway systems for Microsoft 365 to handle outages and disruptions. However, 15 hours before the global Microsoft 365 outage, Teams "failed over" from the alternative networking gateway to the primary one, which supports Exchange Online. This wouldn't usually cause a problem, except for the new defect introduced by the July update.

Finally, Microsoft's servers weren't operating at 100 percent at the time. According to Lamanna, it just so happened that nearly 14 percent of the server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service "due to an unrelated issue from the previous day."

Again, normally, this would have been routine maintenance. The service would still have sufficient capacity to work as normal.

All three issues occurring at once led to disaster.

"Taken together, the increased load and the reduced server capacity, caused the network gateway to encounter the latent bug from July," Lamanna writes. "This caused requests to build up until servers ultimately stopped responding. This occurred during the peak window of traffic in the United States."

Recovery from the outage also took much longer than usual because servers were "immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and became unresponsive again." In addition, Microsoft was unable to roll back the code because the bug dated back to July. So, Microsoft essentially had to develop a patch within that short timeframe, which returned the code to its previous "good state."

The entire explanation from Microsoft is actually quite an interesting read and shows that no matter how big the company is, massive tech issues can still occur. Readers can check out Lamanna's entire post on X; Microsoft enterprise customers can also learn more in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center.

Microsoft has since apologized for the outage. Businesses affected by the downtime can also file a claim with the company for credits due to the downtime.

#585. What is vibe manufacturing? AI projects are leaving the chat

The next wave of AI projects might just arrive in the mail.

As AI tools become more capable, people are asking chatbots to help design things they can hold, wear, or install in their homes, from custom jewelry and household gadgets to metal parts built around precise measurements.

Welcome to "vibe manufacturing." The phrase borrows from "vibe coding," where people describe the software they want and ask AI to help create it. Here, the goal is a physical object, with AI helping develop a design that can be printed at home or sent to a manufacturer.

The appeal is easy to understand. Most people have encountered a product that would be perfect if it were a little smaller, worked differently, or fit that one awkward space. These tools offer a starting point for making their own version. Getting it right, though, still takes more than a good prompt.

Vibe manufacturing loosely describes using conversational AI to help design and build physical things. Someone explains what they want, supplies measurements or reference images, and works with an AI tool to develop it. Depending on the project, that could involve generating a digital model, choosing components, writing software for a device, or figuring out assembly.

The bridge between the conversation and the object is often CAD, short for computer-aided design. CAD software creates precise digital designs for physical objects, and AI tools can help translate everyday requests into the code or geometry behind them.

Entrepreneur Greg Isenberg outlines the process in an Oct. 4 explainer on X. "You describe what you want. An AI turns it into a precise design file. A printer on your desk tests it overnight," he writes.

Tools such as the open-source text-to-cad project support that process, providing workflows for creating models with AI agents, producing engineering drawings, and checking designs for fabrication. The resulting files can go to a printer or an outside shop with the equipment to make the parts.

Some of the projects getting attention solve problems that are deeply specific to their creators.

In October, entrepreneur and former X head of product Nikita Bier posted that he'd used AI to design a dog door with a Wi-Fi-controlled lock, customized to his house. Despite having no background in metal fabrication or electrical engineering, he said it was being manufactured for almost the same price as a mass-produced alternative. "We are now entering into an era where any product can be created exactly to a consumer's preferences & needs," he wrote.

Other makers are tackling repairs. In a post on r/ApolloScooters, one Reddit user described using Claude to modify an existing design file after their scooter’s rear fender broke. They ordered a replacement through a 3D-printing service and shared a photo of the result, while noting that they would make the next version shorter.

Around the house, customization can be decorative, too. An employee for AI modeling tool Meshy, Jessica Bergau, used the company's AI tool to design cabinet knobs, then asked Claude to generate a script that added screw threads to the models. A blog post documents her plastic prints and the work needed to get an actual screw to fit. And some projects start with wanting a device that doesn't quite exist on store shelves. In a recent Business Insider report, David Plakon described using AI to help build a homemade answering box so his children could leave messages for their grandparents.

The report also featured a sheet-metal robot arm and a custom steel component for securing a camper to a truck.

Greg Isenberg sees a business opportunity in what he calls "the gadgets nobody would build" — products for audiences too small to interest a large manufacturer. He points to accessories for particular bikes or coffee machines, replacement parts for discontinued products, and equipment tailored to an individual business.

"When the design is a file and the factory makes one at a time, the product can fit you instead," he writes.

That vision extends beyond personal projects to businesses serving small markets. Whether those businesses can consistently deliver reliable products at a workable price is a separate question.

Turning an AI-assisted design into a physical object often relies on existing manufacturing services: SendCutSend lets customers order custom metal parts, Xometry offers processes including machining and 3D printing, and JLCPCB can manufacture and assemble circuit boards. Each requires files specifying what to build.

But access to production equipment doesn’t guarantee a workable design. "A design can look perfect on screen and be impossible to manufacture," Isenberg writes. He recommends checking a manufacturer’s guidelines, testing a physical prototype, and paying a mechanical engineer to review files before ordering.

Dominic Böttger's account of making a case for an air-quality sensor shows why. He used Claude Code to develop the enclosure, but early versions had misplaced supports and an opening wide enough for the circuit board to slide out. Getting it right took seven design revisions and three prints, with photographs helping guide corrections. "The feedback loop needs the physical part," he writes.

Industrial manufacturers face the added challenge of making those results repeatable. Technology and manufacturing organization Automation Alley explores that ambition in its March 2026 Integr8 playbook, Vibe Manufacturing: Where AI Meets Additive. Engineers set requirements such as strength, durability, and cost, then use AI to explore designs for additive manufacturing, the category that includes 3D printing.

"AI explores the options. Additive manufacturing turns those options into physical reality," CEO Tom Kelly writes in the foreword. The report also discusses "Smart Product Recipes," digital instructions intended to standardize production across locations.

As AI tools improve, more people may get the chance to make the products they've been wishing someone would sell. The real test will be how well those ideas hold up once they leave the chat window.

#582. JetBlue unveils new first-class seats to bring back profits

JetBlue Airways unveiled its new domestic first-class seats Wednesday as more of the country's carriers bet on the premium travel boom to make them profitable again.

JetBlue announced it would offer a domestic first class — BlueFirst — in December 2024 and plans to start flying aircraft with the new seats and full on-board product next month. The carrier showed off the new cabin at its home hub at John F. Kennedy International Airport on Wednesday. Retrofits will continue during 2027, CEO Joanna Geraghty told CNBC late last month.

JetBlue will have 12 of the seats on its Airbus A320 fleet and 30 extra-legroom seats, down from 42 of those options previously. Because the airplanes don't have ovens, JetBlue said it is offering an array of cold food options like sesame noodles, pastrami sandwiches and tortellini salad, though they vary by route.

The rollout comes as the New York airline tries to stabilize after last posting a profit in 2019. Last month, JetBlue executives sought to calm investors after shares in the airline hit a record low following a report that bondholders had contracted restructuring advisors.

"We have no intention, no plans to file for bankruptcy. We are not engaged with any restructuring company," Geraghty told CNBC in an interview on Oct. 27.

Geraghty told CNBC's Phil LeBeau on Wednesday that JetBlue has "met with a few of the creditors over the last couple of weeks as part of ... normal investor engagement." She said the company made it clear to bondholders that JetBlue doesn't need to reorganize.

The airline's shares are up more than 40% this month, more than other passenger carriers, as of midday Wednesday, though they are still off about 11% so far this year.

JetBlue is betting that resilient travel demand, especially for roomier seats will help fuel its turnaround plan, which aims to get the carrier to an operating profit next year and $1 in adjusted earnings per share in 2028.

Airline executives have said they expect fares to stay elevated next year as they grapple with higher costs, including but not limited to fuel, such as labor and airport fees. Geraghty said Wednesday that even if fuel prices moderate next year, "I don't think fares are going to fall as much as people expect."

Airlines large and small are racing to outfit their cabins with roomier, more expensive seating options to help cover ever-higher costs, from jet fuel to labor to airport operation fees.

For example, a ticket in the new recliner first-class seats between Kennedy airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport in Florida is going for $847 roundtrip in the first week of March while standard economy is $446.

On Tuesday, budget carrier Frontier Airlines unveiled its new first-class seats, which will take up the first two rows, and said it would outfit its Airbus fleet with premium seating that has extra legroom and in-seat power through row eight. The airline will take out a row of seating on its planes to make the pricier ones fit, Chief Marketing Officer Bobby Schroeter told CNBC in an interview Monday.

JetBlue last month reported that it ended the third quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines.

JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing.

Geraghty told CNBC last month there is a "fundamental disconnect between the narrative in the bond market and what our financial results actually demonstrate."

When asked whether JetBlue's eye on keeping costs down includes furloughs, layoffs or buyouts, Geraghty last month said "absolutely not."

#579. The Bank Outage May Have Nothing to Do With Your Bank

If you were planning to do any banking today, good luck.

Customers of many major financial institutions experienced unspecified technical issues on Monday as thousands of reports flooded the uptime-tracking website Downdetector.com from people saying that they had issues using their banks in some way.

It is currently unclear which systems are having issues. However, the problem may stem from technical difficulties at JPMorganChase, the top retail bank, which holds over 10 percent of all US deposits.

“JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems—there is no evidence this is cyber-related,” says JPMorganChase spokesperson Pablo Rodriguez. “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.”

Rodriguez adds that the bank is not experiencing a “systemic issue” but that “other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.” The spokesperson adds that customers “still have access to their accounts and funds” and that the bank is working to resolve the issues.

Apparent issues with the banks, credit unions, fintech apps, and credit card companies appear to begin around 9:30 am ET and peaked at around 2 pm ET. Many people also reported issues using Zelle, the peer-to-peer money-transfer system adopted by major banks. However, in a statement, Zelle denied its systems were the cause of the reported outages while acknowledging that issues at banks may impact people’s ability to use Zelle.

“Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should,” a Zelle spokesperson says in a statement. “Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds.”

US Bank spokesperson Jeffrey Shelman also says the financial institution’s systems “are not directly impacted.” Shelman adds, however, that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”

Seth Eisen, senior vice president of communications at MasterCard, says, “Our network is operating normally.” A Visa spokesperson says the company is aware of the payments issue, but that Visa’s systems are operating normally. A Capital One spokesperson similarly says the firm “has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time,” while a Bank of America spokesperson says its systems “have been operating normally today.”

According to reports on Downdetector, which is sourced to user reports rather than official statements and may not be accurate, the issues on Monday also impacted customers of Wells Fargo, TD Bank, Navy Credit Federal Union, and more. These companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Eisen, the Mastercard VP, says that DownDetector was “not correct” in the case of his company.

Whatever the cause, the timing of the issues may as well have been designed to get people looking for broader patterns. Last Thursday, Microsoft 365 experienced an unprecedented 24-hour outage that impacted millions of people, governments, businesses, and other institutions globally. Microsoft executive vice president Charles Lamanna said in a post on X on Monday that the outage, which impacted Outlook, Teams, and many other Microsoft cloud services, was related to an update that started rolling out in July but only began causing problems last week.

Soon after Microsoft resolved its outage on Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop order. This time, the issue was related to a problem with Air Traffic Control’s communications systems. “The FAA’s legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding the FAA FTI network, at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” the agency wrote in an FAQ explaining the outage. “This disrupted the system and created instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds.”

The FAA’s five-hour ground stop resulted in thousands of canceled flights and otherwise disrupted travel for countless travelers. The impact of Monday’s banking outage remains unclear.

#577. Amazons cute new Echo Time smart clock is 50% off for Prime members, but not for long

Updated on Nov. 16 at 2:25 p.m. ET — For a limited time, Prime members can get the new Amazon Echo Time smart clock for 50% off. Part of Amazon's early Black Friday sale, this discount makes the smart gadget a lot easier to recommend. Through Nov. 17, Prime members (and only Prime members) can take advantage of an on-page coupon that drops the price to $99.99. On the product page, look for a checkbox that reads, "Exclusive: Get 50% off."

The Echo Time was just released on Oct. 28 alongside a host of new Echo devices, which are getting their first discounts for early Black Friday shoppers.

Keep scrolling to read our original story on the Amazon Echo Time.

Having good taste is expensive. Alas, it has always been thus.

But $200 for a clock is pushing it, even for a snob like me.

That's unfortunate, because I love the design of Amazon's new Echo Time smart alarm.

Earlier this week, Amazon launched a bunch of new Echo smart home devices, and Mashable was there for the unveiling. The new Echo devices have less of a Death Star vibe, and the Echo Time stands out to me for its friendly design. It's exactly the kind of product I can imagine installing on my nightstand.

I really do love the design of this smart alarm. It doesn't have quite the same appeal as the new Apple HomeView for me (I'm not a huge fan of the knitted fabric cover on Amazon smart devices), but the round shape and pleasant, customizable clock faces work extremely well together. I even like the optional stand.

Why does everything have to be so expensive right now? Whether you're booking a hotel, ordering food, buying a phone, or looking for an alarm clock to break your morning phone habits, prices are painful. Amazon's last smart alarm, the Echo Spot, was priced at a much more reasonable $79.99. That is, until Amazon raised prices on the Echo Spot to $109.99 in August. Now, the company is asking us to pay even more. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Echo Time isn't even the only pricey alarm clock I'm lusting after in 2026. Stylish, Instagram-famous analog alarms like the Nanu Arc Alarm Clock cost even more, at $299.

The Echo Time does work really hard to justify the price tag. And, for the record, I really wouldn't be mad about getting this as a Christmas gift this year. I just don't know that I can justify the money myself.

Billed as "your Alexa smart clock," the Echo Time has hundreds of clock faces for its 3.2-inch circular touchscreen, and with the AI-powered Alexa+, you can even use it to control smart lights, set the perfect sleep temperature, or open your blinds. The Echo Time also doubles as a noise machine, playing soothing sounds as you fall asleep at night or meditate in the morning. Amazon says its built-in speaker offers lossless high-definition audio for listening to music.

I've long since learned that having good taste is expensive, but in 2026, having any kind of taste is expensive. This, despite the fact that President Donald Trump promised to bring down prices at the pump, grocery stores, and beyond, telling crowds, "Starting on day one, we will end inflation and make America affordable again." Obviously, that's not what happened. Tech companies, in particular, keep raising prices as they pass along the higher costs of the memory squeeze spurred by the AI industry.

So, you'll have to decide if your budget can bear a $199.99 smart alarm.

My verdict: Wait for Black Friday and see how much the Echo Time is going to cost when it inevitably goes on sale.

#575. The 8 Best Movies to Stream Right Now (November 2026)

November is here, the holidays are approaching, and it’s gotten cold outside—the perfect time of year to cozy up inside with some of the best films gracing streaming services.

This month, there’s plenty of Halloween hangover for horror fans, with viral sensation Backrooms making corridors and empty rooms unimaginably spooky on HBO Max, Thanksgiving carving out a spot for grindhouse connoisseurs on Hulu, and the transgressive Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma proving the genre can have brains and blood over on Mubi.

If you prefer your thrills giant-sized, look no further than Netflix, where the king of monsters can be seen stomping across Japan in the Academy Award–winning Godzilla Minus Zero.

Elsewhere, the Earth itself is in peril in a double bill of animated spectaculars. A warning from the future arrives in the stunning time-travel fantasy Arco, taking viewers on an imaginative journey across centuries on Hulu, while The Day the Earth Blew Up on HBO Max places Looney Tunes icons Daffy Duck and Porky Pig as the planet’s last line of defense. (We’re cooked.)

Here are WIRED’s picks of the best movies to watch right now.

Drawing inspiration from the works of Sylvain Chomet and Studio Ghibli in equal measure, director Ugo Bienvenu has created an absolutely gorgeous piece of animation. This French science fantasy epic follows 10-year-old Arco (Oscar Tresanini in French, Juliano Krue Valdi in English), who time-travels from his home in 2932 in hopes of seeing dinosaurs. Instead, he crashes in 2075, a point where humanity is on the brink of destruction, the planet wracked by brutal storms, its resources all but exhausted, and humanity living in protective bubbles.

Aided by schoolgirl Iris (Margot Ringard Oldra, Romy Fay) and her robot caretaker Mikki, Arco desperately tries to repair his damaged time-suit to return home. However, between environmental devastation, a strange trio hunting him, and his very presence risking the timeline, Arco’s time might be up. Beautiful but somber, Arco is one of the best yet sadly most overlooked films of the year, animated or otherwise.

What good is a kamikaze pilot who survives? That’s the question haunting Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) at the end of WWII, outlasting both the conflict and an encounter with an impossible, dinosaur-like creature on an isolated island. Returning to a devastated Tokyo, the directionless, traumatized Kōichi forms a relationship with fellow survivor Noriko (Minami Hamabe), raising an orphaned baby together. Yet their ad hoc family life is put in the atomic-breath firing line of that strange monster he encountered years earlier, now mutated to colossal size by exposure to atomic tests and stomping angrily onto land. Without weapons, military, or even much of a functioning society, can a still-broken Japan possibly withstand the horror of Godzilla?

While Ichiro Honda’s original 1954 Godzilla was a towering reptilian metaphor for the unknown risks of unleashing nuclear weapons on the world, Godzilla Minus One sees director Takashi Yamazaki leap back almost a decade to explore themes of survivor’s guilt, national despair, and rebuilding community. It’s a kaiju movie with brains, but also a treat for the eyes; it won the Academy Award for Best Visual Effects. With sequel Godzilla Minus Zero in cinemas now, it’s well worth catching up on before seeing Big G throwing down with arch-nemesis King Ghidorah.

When struggling furniture seller Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor) finds a crack in reality in his store’s basement, he becomes obsessed with exploring the seemingly infinite liminal space he’s slipped into. The space goes on forever, yet appears to be entirely empty—apart from an unseen presence stalking him. Becoming obsessed with mapping the unmappable, Clark’s already-fraying life disintegrates further, until his fixation ends up dragging his concerned therapist Mary (Renate Reinsve) into the Backrooms herself—except she doesn’t find it quite so uninhabited. And all the while, someone outside is watching closely.

From internet folklore to cinematic sensation, director Kane Parsons’ Backrooms was the surprise horror hit of the summer. It’s easy to see why—the endless sprawl of impossible corridors and uncanny rooms that connect in ways that seem to defy physics and geometry alike is darkly mesmerizing for viewers, while the unexplained nature of this twisted reality keeps you guessing at every turn. A sequel is in the works, but you can get lost in the Backrooms right now.

When up-and-coming director Kris (Hannah Einbinder) is hired to reboot the floundering Camp Miasma horror franchise, she wants to bring back Billy Presley (Gillian Anderson), the series’ original “Final Girl.” Unsettlingly, Kris finds Billy now living on the abandoned campsite from the dated first flick, living a reclusive life and obsessed with Little Death, the iconic killer from the series. Pitch meetings soon turn into the pair bonding over their fascination with, and experience of, the series—before descending into … well, the hint is in the film’s title.

A festival darling, picking up awards at both Cannes Film Festival and San Sebastián International Film Festival, this smart, transgressive horror outing from director Jane Schoenbrun (We're All Going to the World's Fair, I Saw the TV Glow) cleverly deconstructs the slasher genre and reexamines it from a queer—and extremely meta—perspective.

Somehow, despite a near-century of Looney Tunes cartoons (counting from 1930’s “Sinkin’ in the Bathtub”), The Day the Earth Blew Up is the series’ very first feature-length, fully animated movie (no, Space Jam doesn’t count). It’s been worth the wait, though—this loving pastiche of sci-fi B-movies is a stellar showcase for its top-billed stars, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig (both phenomenally voiced by the sadly departed Eric Bauza).

With an asteroid hurtling toward Earth, UFOs flying around, a sinister scientist meddling with unknown substances, and a zombie plague spread by infected bubble gum, Earth’s last hope is a deranged duck and an anxious pig. We’re probably doomed, but at least we’ll die laughing—this hilarious outing is a reminder of everything great about these beloved characters.

When Yu Kobayashi (Yuzu Aoki) transfers to a new school in rural Japan, he finds the strict culture and rigid conformity of students and staff alike unusual. Classes stand and bow to teachers in unnaturally uniform movements, PE lessons are precise marching practices, and even the hierarchy of bullies and victims seems oddly organized. Initially, Yu writes it off as culture clash in a new environment, until students inexplicably start to form ever-larger human pyramids, with teachers brutally encouraging them. Only Yu and outsider Ai Sato (Anna Yamada) seem able to resist the compulsion to join the pyramid—but with the increasingly maddening adherence to peer pressure spreading across Japan, they might be the only ones.

Director and writer Yûta Shimotsu expands the almost surreal setup into an exploration of conformity and expectations, infusing it all with an uncomfortable dose of J-horror. It’s exceedingly weird in places and demands you make your own conclusions, but at a brisk 81 minutes, it’s a short, sharp, and frequently shocking slice of satire.

Every holiday deserves a related slasher flick—everything from April Fools’ to Christmas to, of course, Halloween. Thanksgiving had been the odd one out, until 2007’s Grindhouse (the anthology double feature coheaded by Robert Rodriguez and Quentin Tarantino), which featured a bunch of mock trailers, including one by Hostel director Eli Roth, centered on a killer Pilgrim. Fast forward to 2023, and Roth finally got the idea out of his head with this full-length version.

A year after a Black Friday riot ends up with a body count, Plymouth, Massachusetts, finds itself stalked by a masked serial killer soon dubbed “John Carver.” The victims: anyone connected with the retail massacre—but the twisted chain of connections between Carver and his kills keeps viewers on their toes throughout. Thanksgiving is unapologetically loyal to the genre, but manages to cram in some sledgehammer-subtle commentary on consumerism alongside the gloriously gratuitous schlock.

When Alma (Maren Eggert) meets Tom (Dan Stevens), he seems perfect. Intelligent, poetic, able to dance—a rare modern gentleman. That is, until he starts glitching, revealing himself as an advanced robot. Initially repulsed, Alma is drawn into a three-week trial of a repaired Tom, testing his capabilities as an assistant and his capacity for emotion. It’s a quietly disconcerting experiment to watch play out, with Alma drawing closer to Tom almost in spite of herself.

First released in 2021, when undetectable AIs and synthetic humanoids were still just about within the realm of fiction, this German sci-fi drama now feels ahead of its time. While I’m Your Man bears some similarities to Alex Garland’s Ex Machina, it’s not as pre-apocalyptic, with director Maria Schrader balancing quasi-romcom tropes with hard existential questions about the nature of intelligence, the quiet banality of AI and robotics infiltrating society, and how we as humans respond.

#574. Could Jensen Huang return to Nvidia? What Trump, Altman, the board are saying.

For 33 years, Nvidia had only one CEO. Now, just days after the chipmaker announced Jensen Huang's resignation, some of the country's biggest names are already want him back — from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman to President Donald Trump.

The decision ultimately belongs to Nvidia's board, which has appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO.

The calls for a comeback follow a week of mounting scrutiny over Huang's intimate extracurriculars. On Nov. 8, Huang had told employees he’d been unfaithful to his wife after reports of a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company that buys Nvidia chips. U.S. officials suspect she had ties to Chinese intelligence, an allegation Beijing has denied. The same day Huang emailed employees, Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. Reuters also reported that Huang had relationships with two Nvidia employees, including one who reported directly to him. Inhales.

It's a lot. But that doesn't mean everyone thinks its enough to get rid of the co-founder permanently. On Nov. 15, Huang was already talking to people close to him about a possible return, according to the Financial Times. One ally told the paper they were getting tech executives together to lobby for his reinstatement and would seek support from the White House.

On Monday, Trump gave that effort some encouragement. "I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters before leaving Washington for the Philippines and China. He said he thought Huang had "learned a big lesson" and questioned whether Alice Huang had worked for Chinese intelligence.

A day earlier, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Larry Kudlow on Fox News that Nvidia should hire its next CEO from outside the company, saying it needed a "dramatic shake-up."

Huang's supporters are also making their case online. "Thirty-three years deserve an answer," reads the Stand With Jensen petition, which demands that Nvidia's board reinstate its co-founder while the independent investigation is underway. "We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process," it adds. If directors think Huang should stay out of the job, the letter asks them to explain what evidence led them to that decision and why it serves Nvidia's interests. It also calls on the board to disclose what the investigation will cover, when it expects to finish, and how Huang will get a chance to respond. By Monday afternoon, the campaign's website showed more than 185,000 signatures, including more than 9,300 from people who identified themselves as current Nvidia employees. The site also lists Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Replit CEO Amjad Masad among the signers.

The push to bring Huang back is familiar territory for OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. OpenAI's board fired him in Nov. 2023, and he returned days later after employees and investors rallied behind him. At Semafor's Silicon Valley & the World event on Monday, Altman said he sympathized with Huang and had long seen him as a hero. When asked whether Huang should get his job back, Altman said, "I don’t think I know enough to answer that question." He added: "it's hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen Huang."

Altman also sounded confident in Nvidia's ability to back the data centers that AI companies depend on. "Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company," he said. "I think people still trust their guarantees very much."

OpenAI has a stake in that confidence. At an Ohio data center campus where an OpenAI affiliate is leasing capacity, Nvidia has agreed to guarantee up to $105 billion in certain lease and power payments if the tenant defaults under conditions spelled out in the deal. The campus is set to run on Nvidia hardware, with limited exceptions.

For now, Kress is running Nvidia on an interim basis while keeping the CFO job she's held since 2013. The board, led by longtime director Harvey C. Jones, says it will consider internal and external candidates. It has already approached Arm CEO Rene Haas, the Financial Times reported.

The next chance to hear from Nvidia's new leadership comes Tuesday at 5 p.m. ET, when the company holds its first earnings call since Huang's departure.

#570. Instagram creators can now earn Amazon commissions right from their posts

Instagram just gave creators one less reason to say "link in bio."

Starting Nov. 16, eligible U.S. creators can now add Amazon affiliate links right to their Reels and feed posts, according to head of Instagram Adam Mosseri, with room for up to 30 products in a Reel and 20 in a feed post.

"A lot of creators make money with affiliate links, but you've mostly had to share them in stories or bio," Mosseri wrote in a post. He added that the feature is "free to add, and we don't take any cut of what you earn."

Creators have long sent followers to a Story, a DM, or their profile to find those links. Now the recommendation and the link can live in the same post. If someone makes a qualifying purchase through the link, Amazon may pay the creator a commission. (Disclosure: Mashable participates in the Amazon affiliate program.)

The rollout is open to U.S. adults with a professional Instagram account and more than 1,000 followers, WIRED reported. To get started, eligible creators can connect their Amazon Influencer account under Monetization in Instagram's Professional Dashboard. From there, tagging an Amazon item automatically adds an affiliate link and an image preview. Creators who connect an Amazon Associates account can also paste a regular Amazon product URL and still get credit for qualifying sales. Before adding an item, creators can see the estimated commission rate for that product. Shoppers who tap a tag can see the product and its price in Instagram, then head to Amazon to check out.

Moving the link closer to the recommendation could make a real difference for creators who earn a commission when someone buys. Instagram told TechCrunch that product links on Reels and feed posts have drawn about twice as many clicks as links in creators' bios. The timing gives creators a chance to see whether those extra clicks turn into sales during Black Friday.

The announcement comes as Instagram's parent company, Meta, was at odds with Amazon over shopping just two months ago. In September, Amazon blocked Muse, Meta's AI assistant, from shopping on its site on behalf of customers.

So will there be more shopping posts in the feed? "We don't expect a sudden influx of shopping content from this launch," Instagram spokesperson Megan Buckley told WIRED, saying the app will keep recommending posts based on what people are likely to find interesting or useful.

It's important to note that YouTube has been doing this for years. Eligible creators have already been able to tag products and earn commissions through YouTube Shopping in 2023, and in August, YouTube added Amazon to the program, giving U.S. creators a way to tag Amazon products in Shorts, longer videos, and livestreams.

The holiday shopping rush will be an early test for Instagram's version of this feature, as your favorite creator's next gift guide in Reels could have a shopping link for every item on the list.

#564. American Airlines brings fresh food back to NY-Chicago first class for first time since 2019

American Airlines said Wednesday it's bringing small, fresh "bites" to first class on flights between its hubs in New York and Chicago, the carrier's latest effort to win over higher-spending customers.

The changes start this month. Customers will be able to pick between two options, which include prosciutto and melon or apple cinnamon chia pudding for breakfast and a Thai noodle salad or mezze plate for lunch and dinner, American said Wednesday.

American last offered fresh food for first class on these routes in 2019, a spokeswoman said. Currently, customers in first class on these flights get a smaller, packaged snack. Airlines largely have limited food options for shorter flights, even in first class.

American has fallen behind Delta Air Lines and United Airlines in profits and investments in premium options. The airline has been working to step up those premium offerings in recent years with new cabins, lounges and plans for seatback screens on its narrow-body fleets.

#558. OpenAI launches tool for finding child sexual abuse material

OpenAI announced Monday the release of a new tool to detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM), including content generated by artificial intelligence.

The tool is a classifier that looks for visual signs of abuse in images. It then scores images to help human reviewers prioritize which of them warrant attention. OpenAI said its CSAM classifier is the first broadly available tool of its kind to include a specific signal indicating the image may be generated with AI.

This capability is becoming critical as AI-generated CSAM skyrockets.

A new analysis conducted by Childlight — Global Child Safety Institute at the University of Edinburgh found AI-related reports of CSAM increased globally by more than 8,400 percent from 2023 to 2025. Last year, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children received more than 400,000 of these reports. In 2023, that number was roughly 4,700.

"Individual companies like OpenAI have a responsibility to prevent our technology from being exploited by predators to harm children, and we also must work together with the broader industry, child safety organizations and law enforcement to advance our collective efforts to protect children online," OpenAI said in its blog post about the announcement.

The company's new tool can be used by organizations required or authorized to detect CSAM, including certain developers that use OpenAI's application programming interface, or API.
